This file contains a summary of the main points from the United States Constitution. The document establishes a bicameral legislature with a Senate (six-year terms) and House of Representatives, which must meet in December for continuity. Both houses require a majority to conduct business, share unique powers over impeachment and revenue bills, and enjoy immunity during sessions. The President is elected for four years as Commander-in-Chief, appointing judges with Senate approval; the legislative process requires presidential signature unless Congress adjourns (becoming law automatically ten days later if not signed). Congress holds significant power under Article III to tax, borrow money, regulate commerce, coin currency, maintain a navy, and exercise exclusive authority over territories. The President can raise armies for two years at a time and govern the militia. The judicial branch is created by Congress with a Supreme Court handling cases involving treaties, states, and citizens. Treason is defined as levying war against the nation or aiding its enemies without evidence from two witnesses or an open confession. No individual can be convicted of treason without such proof. Article IV mandates that each state must respect the records and judicial proceedings of all other states, while allowing Congress to define methods for proving these documents. Additionally, citizens are entitled to full privileges and immunities in their respective states, including protection from forced removal or escaping labor obligations. Summary of all 9 pages.
